card.stem: An entrance porch with a lean-to roof projects 1.8 metres from the external wall of a house. The walls of the porch and of the house are of 450 mm concrete block construction with a full-fill insulated cavity. The external wall of the porch is finished with a rainscreen of 20 mm vertical larch cladding. The highly insulated lean-to roof has a pitch of 30° with a slate finish. The rafters are 200 mm × 50 mm with insulated plasterboard fixed to the underside of the sloping rafters.
card.questionText: To a scale of 1:10, draw a vertical section through the entrance porch showing the external wall of the porch, the sloping roof, and the front wall of the house. Include the typical construction details of the porch from a point 300 mm below the wall plate, through the sloping rafters, to a level 350 mm above the abutment of the porch roof with the front wall of the house. Show three courses of slate at eaves.

rows.verbatim: External wall and eaves - typical detailing
rows.contextNote: Best four details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Marking menu: larch cladding rain screen; battens/counter battens; cavity wall blockwork and low-conductivity wall ties; full-fill insulation; cavity closer; wallplates; skim/plaster.

Best four details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Marking menu: fascia/soffit/gutter (any two); three courses of slate; slating battens 50 × 30 mm at 400 mm centres and counter battens; roof breather membrane; ventilation; rafter and insulation; air barrier membrane and airtightness taping; insulated plasterboard (50 mm insulation + 12.5 mm plasterboard).

rows.verbatim: Front wall of house and abutment - typical detailing
rows.contextNote: Best four details, 4 each (3 for drawing, 1 for annotation). Marking menu: external and internal render; full-fill cavity blockwork and low-conductivity wall ties; concrete lintels; cavity closer; rafter support; stepped DPC; lead flashing (under and apron).

card.stem: The design of a house should be flexible to meet the changing needs of the occupants over their lifetime.
card.questionText: Discuss in detail, using notes and freehand sketches, two best practice guidelines for each of the following areas when designing a house for lifetime use: kitchen; bedroom.

rows.contextNote: Notes 3 and sketches 3. Such as: 1200–1500 mm between opposing work surfaces; angled or pop-up sockets that are easy to see and reach; D-handles at least 100 mm long; cupboard doors opening to at least 135 degrees; hot water to the sink no hotter than 40 °C with sensor or lever taps.

A second, different kitchen guideline: notes 3 and sketches 3. Such as: clear knee space beneath the sink and hob for a seated user; oven and fridge in a housing at an accessible height; worktops adjustable between 760 and 900 mm; at least 300 mm beside the hob; pull-out drawers in deep base units; a level threshold to the garden.

Notes 3 and sketches 3. Such as: at least 800 mm clear either side of the bed and more at its end; a 1500 mm turning circle; sockets and switches 400–1000 mm above floor level; switches at the door and both sides of the bed.

A second, different bedroom guideline: notes 3 and sketches 3. Such as: windows operable with one hand, levers 800–1200 mm high; a ground-floor room usable as a bedroom; a soft spot in the wall to the bathroom for a future en suite door; hard spots for a future hoist.

card.stem: The drawing shows the front elevation and ground floor plan of a house with an adjoining disused forge. The forge was built using natural local stone with a red corrugated steel pitched roof. The wall A-A is south facing and the wall B-B has views to the mountains. The owners intend to convert the forge into an open-plan kitchen/dining and living space. Consideration at the design stage is to be given to: linking the existing kitchen to the forge; optimising natural daylight; maximising the views to the mountains.
card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, show a revised internal layout for the proposed renovation of the forge shown, that incorporates each of the above requirements. Justify your design choices.

rows.verbatim: Revised internal layout for the kitchen/dining and living area
rows.contextNote: Notes and freehand sketches of a coherent open-plan kitchen/dining and living layout in the forge. Such as: structural steel in the gable at the junction of the house and forge, making the kitchen and forge one space, or keeping a section of the gable wall to define the spaces; a kitchen island at the centre of the new space; the dining table beside the large glazing.

rows.verbatim: Linking existing kitchen to the forge
rows.contextNote: The existing kitchen linked to the forge, for example by opening the gable at the junction with structural steel, keeping the kitchen in place to save moving services.
Daylight optimised, for example glass doors in wall A-A for southern light, floor-to-ceiling south glazing, or ridge/roof glazing units.

rows.verbatim: Maximising the views to the mountain
rows.contextNote: The mountain views maximised, for example large high-performance glazing in the gable towards wall B-B.

The design choices justified, for example heat and light flowing through one open space, solar gain from the south, retained window positions keeping the vernacular character, triple or quadruple low-e glazing for comfort and less glare.

rows.contextNote: A clear table of the materials with their conductivity or resistivity, thickness in metres and resistance.

card.questionText: Using notes and freehand sketches, discuss the importance of any two of the following when carrying out a retrofit to achieve the EnerPHit Passive House design standard: airtightness; windows; building fabric.

rows.verbatim: Discuss the importance of any two in EnerPHit design standard
rows.contextNote: Any two of the three, each notes 6 and sketches 6 = 12. EnerPHit is reached through the five Passive House principles (insulation, limited thermal bridging, triple glazing, airtightness, MVHR), modelled in the PHPP design tool; its space heating demand limit is 25 kWh/m² per year (Passive House 15). Airtightness: Air leakage prevented with airtightness membranes, airtight boards and tapes in timber frame and roofs, and a sand-cement scratch coat, plaster and airtightness paint in block walls; checks for leakage at each stage and a full airtightness test at the end; the EnerPHit target is under 1.0 air changes per hour at 50 Pascals (Passive House 0.6); without airtightness the insulation cannot perform. Windows: Passive House triple-glazed windows of 0.80 W/m²K or less (EnerPHit, installed, 0.85 W/m²K or less); frames in line with the external insulation to avoid a thermal bridge; shading and ventilation planned against summer overheating. Building fabric: Insulation increased to roof, floor and walls (U-value 0.120 W/m²K or less for EnerPHit) by cavity, external or internal insulation; quality workmanship to avoid thermal bridges; external insulation continued below ground level; airtightness and insulation achieved together.
